newsitem.title: UK: Fenchurch fuels insurance fears with div cut.
newsitem.headline: Fenchurch fuels insurance fears with div cut.

text.p: British insurance broker Fenchurch Plc on Friday fuelled conerns about future profitability in the overcrowded insurance broking market, when it reported a sharp drop in profits and more than halved its final dividend.

Chairman Rupert Hambro blamed "over-capacity and intense competition" for a slide in full-year pre-tax pre-exceptional profits to 5.9 million stg from 8.1 million and a cut in the final dividend to 2.75 pence per share from 5.75 pence.
The dividend cut was not wholly unexpected, but has raised doubts over future performance. Merrill Lynch cut its pre-tax profits forecast for 1997 to 6.5 million stg from 7.4 million.

Commenting on the dividend cut, Fenchurch's chief executive Michael Small told Reuters in an interview: "We have to look at the position as it is today, what we've done in the past year and where we're going to go in the future and we're cautious."
"We have to be cautious in our industry. We're being very prudent, we believe, and prudence is governing our decisions."
An underlying rise in expenses this year of nearly five percent has done little to convince most insurance analysts that the broker is doing enough to control costs.

But Small said growth in costs was slowing and employee numbers had been reduced by seven percent since last December. Fenchurch would continue to selectively shed staff next year. Analysts said the depressing figures should not be viewed in isolation. Other insurance broking operations have offered the stock market dismal food for thought in recent weeks with profit warnings, restructuring and job losses dominating the sector.
"It's the environment which we are in at the moment, which is tougher than any of us have ever seen it," said Small.

Industry executives and analysts alike are predicting a massive shakeout among the quoted insurance brokers with a few cash rich global giants like U.S.-based Aon Corp seen capable of expanding by acquisition, while profiting from the demise of other smaller, less well-capitalised competitors.

The departure just over two months ago of Fenchurch's head of North American operations, John Plummer, for rival Benfield Ellinger, has been interpreted by analysts as one example of how industry-wide consolidation could begin to affect companies.

When valuing insurance brokers, the market places emphasis on management and the business key figures bring or take away with them. Prominent individuals and teams are regarded almost as assets. Share prices will react if changes affect earnings.

In Plummer's case, Fenchurch stressed that it had not lost any revenue. But it emerged on Friday that the broker is clearly peeved enough to have slapped down a court order effectively barring Plummer from working in the insurance market for a year, following which he will face further restrictions. When Plummer sold over 200,000 Fenchurch shares in June, the shares fell from 110 pence to 94 over a period of three days.

They closed a penny higher at 59 on Friday. Robin Savage at Credit Lyonnais Laing, although unenthusiastic about the stock, said investors might see value in the company being taken out by a UK or U.S. company as part of the anticipated consolidation.
